t: Thousand Separator - Placing Dots Every Three Digits
o: We need the decimal digits of n with a dot inserted after every third digit counted from the right: 1234 becomes 1.234, while 987 needs no separator at all. The mental model is chunking the digit string into groups of three anchored at the least significant end, then joining the groups with dots. Because n is below 2^31, the string has at most ten digits, so performance is a non-issue; correctness lives in the edge cases - n = 0, and numbers whose leading chunk is shorter than three digits.
k: Separators anchor to the right end, so walk digits right-to-left and drop a dot after every third digit taken.
n = 0 must yield "0"; arithmetic chunk loops never execute for it, so guard it explicitly.
Equivalently peel blocks with n % 1000; every block except the most significant one needs zero-padding to width 3.

a.i: Convert n to its decimal string and traverse it backwards, copying characters into a buffer and appending a dot after every third copied digit, except when the copy just made was the final (leftmost) character. Reversing the buffer at the end restores reading order. This mirrors exactly how humans place thousands separators and is hard to get wrong.
s: Scan from the last character to the first, keeping a count of copied digits.
After every third digit, append a dot unless the scan is finished.
Reverse the buffer and return it as the answer.
a.t: O(d) - the at-most-10 digits of n are each processed once.
a.sp: O(d) - the output buffer of digits and dots.

a.i: Treat the number as base-1000 digits: repeatedly take n % 1000 as the next block and divide n by 1000 until it reaches zero. The last block extracted is the most significant and prints as-is; every lower block must be padded back to three digits with leading zeros, so 1000000 renders as 1.000.000 rather than 1.0.0. Handle n = 0 up front because the extraction loop never runs for it.
s: Return "0" immediately when n is zero.
Repeatedly record str(n % 1000) and set n to n divided by 1000.
Start the answer with the last recorded (most significant) block.
Append a dot and the zero-padded block for each remaining block, popping in reverse.
a.t: O(d) - one constant-time extraction per three-digit block.
a.sp: O(d) - the block list and the output string.

w: Either solution is interview-ready: the string scan is the safest to implement under pressure, while modulo chunking demonstrates number sense; in production you would simply reach for locale-aware formatting. Pitfalls: forgetting to pad middle blocks (1000000 must print 1.000.000, not 1.0.0), emitting a leading dot for inputs below 1000, and overlooking n = 0. Likely follow-ups: support negative integers by prefixing a minus sign to the formatted absolute value, or swap the separator and grouping per locale.
